cells.tense: You are the one walking into the fog first, and you are doing it now.
cells.ask: Pick one open question — not the whole path — and say out loud what you'll do about it before the week turns.
cells.core: You don't need the whole road to start walking. That isn't recklessness — you've learned the difference between forcing an answer and meeting what's actually in front of you. You pick a direction in the mist and the next step shows itself. That's the shape of it when it's going well: moving first with your eyes open. Right now you're inside that. Someone has to go ahead of the group and you've taken it, which is why things move around you. The piece that feeds this — the part that keeps it from tipping — is letting yourself not know the answers yet, letting what you perceive arrive fresh instead of sourced from what you already believe. Somebody can tell you something you didn't expect, and it lands because you're still listening. That's what keeps the charge honest.
cells.sheetLine: You walk first and stay open — both, at the same time.
cells.verb: moving first through fog too thick to see the far side
cells.place: a door you can't see the other room through

cells.tense: You are already living in the far side of this and dragging the present there with you.
cells.ask: Name the outcome you're charging toward, then ask one person this week what they see from where they stand instead of what should happen next.
cells.core: You've seen the other room. It's clear to you — the version where this is done, resolved, finished — so you're pushing toward it before anyone has agreed to go. The charge is real and it isn't rushing for its own sake. But you're carrying an outcome that hasn't been written yet, and treating it like it's already true. That's where it tips. The group isn't behind you because they can't see what you see. You're calling it clarity. It might be speed. Nothing wrong with speed, but somewhere the watching turned into a strategy, and the strategy is going to drive what you say next before anyone in the room gets to say theirs. Understanding that shows you something new isn't available when you're holding the ending open as settled. Ease the grip on the ending for one conversation.
cells.sheetLine: The ending is easy to see and it isn't decided yet.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door you haven't opened and you are there right now.
cells.ask: Tomorrow, do the smallest concrete thing with the one open question instead of researching it — one call, one file, one line.
cells.core: There's something you've been looking at without stepping toward. Not vague — specific. You can probably name the thing you haven't done. The watching happens, the wish happens, the move doesn't. Whatever the reason, the forward charge has gone somewhere else. It's sitting in things you can build slowly, quietly, without declaring anything. That builds — it just doesn't touch the open question, and it can't, because the open question is the one you're backing away from. What pulls it back isn't more deciding or more willing. It's engaging with something concrete, small, doable, and letting that open the way back to the forward move. One thing tomorrow. Not the whole path.
cells.sheetLine: The forward pressure stopped and the ground is fine without it.

cells.tense: You are already charting the way through and calling it something other than what you're doing.
cells.ask: Take one decision you've been saying is obvious or the team's, and write or say a sentence starting with 'I think' about it.
cells.core: You might say this is obvious — as if the direction got decided on its own, or as if it's what anyone would do in the room. Meanwhile you've been shaping the route the whole time, steering without taking your hand on the wheel. The steering does its work. The credit doesn't get claimed. That's fine for a while, then it gets expensive: you can't tell your own moves from the situation's moves, and the people around you can't either, so the fog around the question thickens instead of clearing. There's a simpler version of this you've stepped past. Not the whole leadership thing — the earlier, quieter move of naming what you see and letting that be how the change starts. Say one of them out loud, small.
cells.sheetLine: You've been leading this without saying you picked a direction.

attempts.check: The record's 'authority through intent' reads as charge-and-command, but the seat is imagination — navigating ambiguity. The reader might say 'I'm not a leader' or 'I just pull people along.' The medicine is cognition-seated both times — Initiate in balance, Catalyst of Abstraction in excess — so the ask must stay an act of seeing or naming, not of pushing. The sentence that serves me more than them: any line where I describe them as born to lead; the card is a behavior, not a destiny.
